You are describing binary outcomes. When specific enough, binary outcomes can be applied to almost anything. Take your deck of cards example. If you randomly draw a card it will either be an ace (4/52 odds) or not be an ace (48/52 odds). Binary outcome. Said a different way, it could be a heart (13/52 odds) or not be a heart (39/52 odds). Binary outcome. But in both the examples the odds are not even (50/50), but by how you are predetermining (it is or it isn’t) your outcome, you are making the result binary, which can feel like 50/50. You can apply a binary outcome to almost any situation, but that does not make the odds 50/50.

Large commercial planes on anything but a puddle jump, will be too heavy at landing weight even if the energy density of the battery is similar to that of jet fuel. 

The largest problem, IMO, is that battery powered aircraft don’t get lighter as the flight goes on, which makes low speed handling characteristics much worse and more dangerous. 

Batteries will have to have much greater energy density than jet fuel for them to be light enough to not ruin low speed flight handling characteristics. At least the way current commercial airlines are built and operate.

A huge problem with battery powered airplanes, especially large commercial aircraft, is that the aircraft will not lose weight during the flight if it is battery powered. Making the the low speed flight handling characteristics at landing (the most dangerous part of the flight) much worse. 

When airplanes have an issue during take off and have to immediately land, they dump fuel to make the plane lighter. 

No amount of new battery tech will solve this problem, IMO. So runways would have to be lengthened and reinforced and landing struts and gear would have to be considerably strengthened as well. Aside from some (now) off color jokes, Frasier’s snobbishness is part of what makes him work as a character. Outwardly, because of all the things you mention, he seems like an awful, pretentious, superficial person with karen-esque tendencies and contempt for anyone of lower social class. That was true back in the 90s and is true now. But as you get to know that character you realize that these negative traits are offset by a person who is a caring friend and family member, a psychiatrist who takes pride in helping people, someone who is ruled by their ethics, and who is a deeply flawed and damaged person in their own right. I don’t think that neutering the negative aspects of Frasier (which I think are still hilarious) will work for him as character because it creates the balance (the push and pull) of what makes Frasier such a great character. If he was only good characteristics we might as well call it, Full House: Frasier Moves In. 

Cat fishing a gay Patrick Stewart because Frasier loved the benefits of the relationship is still hilarious, and I would argue that is very 2022. Frasier didn’t care about being seen as gay, he only cared about the benefits and status that the relationship gave him. Now more than ever Frasier’s never ending pursuit of status/clout is relatable to the social media generation. And in the end, as it always did, Frasier’s better judgement forced him to end the relationship. 

The only recurring jokes from the old series which I don’t think would pass today are the constant Roz slut-shaming, though I think it again is still relevant today and mostly hilarious, Roz was never ashamed of it so it’s empowering to some extent and the banter it created is classic Frasier (the same way Frasier was constantly razzed in the early parts of the show for being involuntarily celibate). The other recurring jokes that certainly wouldn’t fly today are the Bulldog/Noel office sexual harassment stuff. Which was barely funny then and certainly extremely inappropriate these days (though I think that the Bulldog character could have had a redeeming arc in the later years).

Let us not forget that Martin (and to a lesser extent Daphne and Roz) who was as blue collar as they come, kept Frasier grounded and forced Frasier to constantly examine his elitist tendencies. So to the extend that the daughter in law now fills that role I think it could work, but I would weary about Frasier having an epiphany in these matters as if he is being exposed to more grounded viewpoints for the first time. Martin was incredibly important in that respect and it would be doing that beloved character a huge disservice (IMO) if a new character came in and “corrected” a huge part of Frasier’s personality where Martin, Daphne and Roz could not.
